title: RESTful API Design
learningObjectives: Identify the right questions before designing an API
Design resource-oriented URLs with proper HTTP verbs and status codes
Anticipate API abuse and failure modes
Evaluate trade-offs in API design decisions
keyTradeoffs: REST vs GraphQL for different consumer needs
Synchronous response vs async with polling for long operations
commonPitfalls: Using verbs in URLs instead of resource nouns
Returning 200 for all responses with error in the body
Leaking stack traces in error responses
transferPrompt: You've designed the API. Now a breaking change is needed. How would you version it? What are the options (URL path, header, query param) and what are the trade-offs of each?

1.coachQuestion: You're asked to design a RESTful API. Before jumping into endpoints, what questions would you ask to clarify the requirements?

junior.point: Who are the consumers (web frontend, mobile app, third-party developers)?
Is this a public, internal, or partner API?
What operations are needed (CRUD, search, bulk)?
What authentication method will be used (OAuth, API keys, cookies)?

mid.point: Expected request volume and peak traffic patterns?

senior.point: API governance: who owns the contract, how are changes approved?
Backward compatibility requirements and deprecation policy?
Documentation strategy (OpenAPI spec-first)?
Multi-tenant considerations (data isolation in responses)?
SLA requirements (latency targets, uptime guarantees)?

modelAnswer.junior: Before designing endpoints, I'd ask: What resources are we exposing (users, products, orders)? Who consumes this — our own frontend, a mobile app, or third parties? Is it public or internal? What operations — just CRUD or also search, bulk updates, aggregations? What auth — API keys, OAuth, session cookies? These determine the URL structure, response formats, and security model.
modelAnswer.mid: Beyond the basics: What's the expected volume — 100 requests/min or 10,000? This affects caching strategy and rate limiting. Which resources are read-heavy vs write-heavy? Do we need real-time updates (webhooks for third parties, SSE for our frontend)? How large are collections — we need pagination, but should it be offset-based (simple) or cursor-based (consistent under writes)?
modelAnswer.senior: At the organizational level: Who owns the API contract — is it spec-first (OpenAPI written before code) or code-first? What's the deprecation policy — how long do we support old versions? For multi-tenant APIs: how is data isolated in responses (tenant ID in path vs header)? What are the SLA commitments — p99 latency targets, uptime guarantees? These determine whether we need an API gateway, contract testing, and versioning strategy.

7.coachQuestion: Design the API contract for your resources. What endpoints would you define, and what does a request/response look like?

junior.point: HTTP verbs map to operations: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove)
Semantic status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Error
Consistent response envelope: { data } on success, { error: { code, message } } on failure

mid.point: Filtering and sorting via query params (?status=active&sort=-created_at)
Partial updates with PATCH (send only delta fields) vs PUT (idempotent full replacement)
Idempotency-Key header for POST operations to prevent duplicate creation on network retries
Resource nesting: flat resources with query filters (/orders?userId=123) over deep hierarchies

senior.point: Content negotiation (Accept and Content-Type headers for JSON / binary payloads)
API versioning strategy: URI path (/v1/users) vs custom headers vs Accept header
Batch / bulk operations design with atomic vs partial failure reporting
Standard rate limit response headers (RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset)
Conditional requests via ETag and If-None-Match headers (returning 304 Not Modified to save egress)

modelAnswer.junior: I'd use resource-oriented URLs with HTTP verbs: GET /users (list), GET /users/:id (detail), POST /users (create, returns 201), PATCH /users/:id (update), DELETE /users/:id (delete, returns 204). Every response follows a consistent shape: { data: T } for success, { error: { code: 'VALIDATION_ERROR', message: '...' } } for errors. Status codes are semantic — 400 for bad input, 401 for auth required, 404 for not found, 500 for server errors (never leak stack traces).
modelAnswer.mid: Beyond CRUD: List endpoints need pagination — I'd use cursor-based (GET /users?cursor=abc&limit=20 → response includes { data, nextCursor, hasMore }). Filtering via query params: GET /users?status=active&sort=-created_at. PATCH for partial updates (only send changed fields). POST endpoints accept an Idempotency-Key header to prevent duplicate creation on retry. For nested resources, I prefer flat with filters (/orders?userId=123) over deep nesting (/users/:id/orders/:orderId/items) — it keeps URLs manageable.
modelAnswer.senior: For production APIs: version in the URL path (/v1/users) — it's the most explicit and cacheable option. Bulk endpoints (POST /v1/users/batch) accept arrays with per-item error reporting. Rate limit headers on every response (standard IETF RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset, plus legacy X-RateLimit-* aliases). ETag headers on GET responses enable conditional requests — the client sends If-None-Match, server returns 304 Not Modified if unchanged (saves bandwidth). For spec-first development, define the OpenAPI spec before writing code, then generate validation middleware from the spec.

8.coachQuestion: What could go wrong with your API? Think about invalid input, abuse, and failure scenarios.

junior.point: Input validation on every endpoint (schema validation with types, required fields, size bounds)
Structured error responses that never leak raw stack traces or internal environment variables
Rate limiting to prevent abuse and brute force
Authentication and authorization checks enforced on every protected route
Request payload body size limits (e.g. 1MB cap) to guard against memory exhaustion

mid.point: Malformed JSON handling: return 400 Bad Request, never trigger an unhandled 500 crash
Type coercion vulnerabilities and loose comparison bugs
CORS configuration: explicit whitelist of allowed origins and headers, avoid wildcard * in production
Over-fetching and data exposure: serialize explicit response DTOs rather than raw ORM entities
429 Too Many Requests response with standard Retry-After header

senior.point: Distributed rate limiting with token bucket / sliding window algorithms across multi-node clusters
Abuse detection: identifying scraping bots, sequential identifier enumeration, and distributed attacks
Circuit breaker patterns for downstream microservices and third-party dependencies
Graceful degradation (fallback cached responses or degraded modes when dependencies fail)
Audit logging for sensitive administrative and state-mutating actions
Zero-downtime API key and secret rotation procedures

modelAnswer.junior: Four categories of failure: (1) Invalid input — validate every field on every endpoint with a schema (Zod, Joi). Return 400 with a structured error, never a 500 with stack trace. (2) Abuse — rate limit all endpoints (e.g., 100 requests/minute per user). (3) Auth — check authentication and authorization on every protected route. A missing auth check on one endpoint is a security hole. (4) Size limits — cap request body size (e.g., 1 MB) to prevent memory exhaustion.
modelAnswer.mid: Beyond validation: handle malformed JSON gracefully (return 400, not crash). Watch for type coercion — '0', null, undefined can behave differently. Lock down CORS — never use * in production; whitelist your own domains. Don't over-fetch: if your ORM loads all columns, your API might return password hashes. Use a serialization layer that explicitly lists returned fields. Return 429 with Retry-After header so clients know when to retry.
modelAnswer.senior: At scale: rate limiting needs to be distributed (Redis-backed, not in-memory per server). Detect scraping patterns (sequential ID enumeration, rapid pagination crawls). Implement circuit breakers for downstream dependencies — if the payment service is down, return partial data with a degradation notice, don't let every request hang. Audit log all sensitive operations (data access, permission changes). Plan for API key rotation: support two active keys simultaneously during rotation windows.

9.coachQuestion: What are the key trade-offs you'd evaluate when designing this API? Pick at least two and explain both sides.

junior.point: REST vs GraphQL: REST (simple, standard caching, predictable) vs GraphQL (flexible client-specified shapes, resolves over-fetching, complex parsing)
Data serialization: JSON (universal, human-readable) vs Protobuf/gRPC (compact binary, fast serialization, typed schema)
Nested resources (/users/:id/orders) vs flat resources with filters (/orders?userId=123)
Plural vs singular naming consistency across the API surface

mid.point: Offset pagination (simple, random access, broken on concurrent writes) vs cursor pagination (stable keyset, scalable, no arbitrary page jumps)
Synchronous HTTP execution vs asynchronous job submission with status polling / webhook callbacks
Fine-grained endpoints (many micro-requests) vs coarse-grained endpoints (richer payloads, fewer roundtrips)

senior.point: API Gateway pattern (centralized auth, rate limiting, routing) vs direct service exposure
Internal service protocols: gRPC for service-to-service vs universal REST over HTTP/2
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern tailored per client platform vs a unified general-purpose API
Event-driven updates (Webhooks / SSE / WebSockets) vs polling strategies for real-time state changes
Spec-first OpenAPI development with contract validation vs code-first implementation

modelAnswer.junior: Two key trade-offs: (1) REST vs GraphQL — REST is simpler, widely understood, and inherently cacheable (GET requests). GraphQL lets clients request exactly what they need (no over-fetching), but adds complexity (query parsing, depth limiting, N+1 problems). For a standard CRUD app, REST is usually the right choice. GraphQL shines when many different clients need different data shapes. (2) Nested vs flat resources — /users/:id/orders feels natural but creates deep URLs. Flat /orders?userId=123 is simpler to implement and more flexible for filtering.
modelAnswer.mid: Pagination is a critical trade-off: offset-based (page=3&limit=20) is simple and allows jumping to any page, but it breaks when data is inserted/deleted between pages (items shift). Cursor-based (cursor=abc123&limit=20) is consistent and scales to billions of records, but you can't jump to 'page 5'. For most APIs, cursor pagination is worth the slightly harder client implementation.
modelAnswer.senior: Architecture-level: an API gateway (Kong, AWS API Gateway) centralizes auth, rate limiting, and routing — but adds latency and a single point of failure. For internal services, gRPC is faster (binary, streaming, code generation) but loses REST's browser-friendliness and cacheability. The BFF pattern (one API per client type) prevents mobile from downloading desktop-sized payloads, but multiplies the API surface to maintain.
